hints: Think about what makes the d block special, focus on the electron configuration of the ion formed, not just the atom.
walkthrough:
Remember the precise Cambridge definition**
Do not just say it has d electrons. Many d block metals like zinc and scandium are not counted as transition elements. The key test is whether a stable ion exists where the d orbitals are partly, but not fully, filled.
Final answer: A transition element is an element that forms at least one stable ion with a partially filled d subshell.

hints: Compare a typical transition metal like iron with a Group 1 metal like sodium for strength of metallic bonding and atomic packing.
walkthrough:
Picture the metallic lattice**
Transition metals can use both $(n-1)d$ and $ns$ electrons in metallic bonding, giving stronger attraction between cations and delocalised electrons. Their atoms are also smaller and pack more closely, so mass per unit volume is greater. That is why both melting point and density are higher.
Final answer: Transition elements have higher melting points and higher densities than s-block elements.

hints: Start by recalling that $E^{\ominus}_{cell}$ is a voltage measured between two half-cells, not for a single half-cell alone.
List what standard conditions means for concentration, gas pressure and temperature.
walkthrough:
Define the voltage idea**
Think of two different half-cells joined together. Each has its own tendency to gain or lose electrons. The voltmeter reads the difference between those two electrode potentials. That difference is the cell potential.

Add the word standard**
Standard means every substance is in its standard state so values can be compared. That is $1 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ for all aqueous ions, 1 atm for any gas, and 298 K. Pure solids and liquids are already in standard state.

Final answer: The emf / potential difference between two half-cells under standard conditions.
All solutions $1 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$, gases at 1 atm and temperature 298 K.

hints: Decide which half-cell needs an inert Pt electrode because both species are in solution, and which can use the metal itself as the electrode.
Recall the two external connections needed between half-cells, one for ion flow and one for electron flow with voltage measurement.
List all six components that must be labelled: two electrodes, three solutions and the two external links.
walkthrough:
Sort the electrodes**
The copper half-cell is simple, $\text{Cu}(\text{s})$ dipping into $\text{Cu}^{2+}(\text{aq})$ acts as its own electrode. The iron half-cell has no solid metal, both $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ and $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ are aqueous, so you must add an inert $\text{Pt}(\text{s})$ wire to carry electrons without reacting.

Complete the circuit**
Join the two solutions with a salt bridge to allow ion migration and maintain charge balance. Join the two electrodes with a wire through a voltmeter to measure $E_{cell}$ while allowing electron flow.

Check the labels**
A full mark diagram shows $\text{Pt}$, $\text{Fe}^{2+}(\text{aq})$, $\text{Fe}^{3+}(\text{aq})$ on one side, $\text{Cu}(\text{s})$, $\text{Cu}^{2+}(\text{aq})$ on the other side, plus salt bridge and voltmeter.
Final answer: Pt(s) in $\text{Fe}^{2+}(\text{aq})$ and $\text{Fe}^{3+}(\text{aq})$ half-cell connected via salt bridge and voltmeter to $\text{Cu}(\text{s})$ in $\text{Cu}^{2+}(\text{aq})$ half-cell.

hints: Think of the catalyst as first oxidising one reactant then being regenerated by oxidising the other, write the $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ with $\text{I}^{-}$ step first.
Now write the second step where the $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ formed is oxidised back to $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ by $\text{S}_{2}\text{O}_{8}^{2-}$.
walkthrough:
See why the direct reaction is slow**
$\text{S}_{2}\text{O}_{8}^{2-}$ and $\text{I}^{-}$ are both negative, so they repel. $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ provides two faster steps involving oppositely charged ions.

Write the catalytic cycle**
First $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ oxidises iodide: $$2\text{I}^{-} + 2\text{Fe}^{3+} \rightarrow \text{I}_{2} + 2\text{Fe}^{2+}$$ Then peroxodisulfate regenerates the catalyst by oxidising $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ back: $$\text{S}_{2}\text{O}_{8}^{2-} + 2\text{Fe}^{2+} \rightarrow 2\text{SO}_{4}^{2-} + 2\text{Fe}^{3+}$$ Adding the two steps cancels $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ / $\text{Fe}^{2+}$, proving catalysis.

Final answer: $2\text{I}^{-} + 2\text{Fe}^{3+} \rightarrow \text{I}_{2} + 2\text{Fe}^{2+}$
$\text{S}_{2}\text{O}_{8}^{2-} + 2\text{Fe}^{2+} \rightarrow 2\text{SO}_{4}^{2-} + 2\text{Fe}^{3+}$

hints: Quote the three relevant $E^{\ominus}$ values for $\text{I}_{2}$/$\text{I}^{-}$, $\text{Fe}^{3+}$/$\text{Fe}^{2+}$ and $[\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_{6}]^{3-}$/$[\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_{6}]^{4-}$.
Compare oxidising strengths by $E^{\ominus}$ values, the more positive $E^{\ominus}$ oxidises the system with the less positive $E^{\ominus}$, or calculate $E^{\ominus}_{cell}$.
walkthrough:
Collect the data**
From the Data Booklet: $$E^{\ominus}(\text{I}_{2}/\text{I}^{-}) = +0.54 \text{ V}$$ $$E^{\ominus}(\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe}^{2+}) = +0.77 \text{ V}$$ $$E^{\ominus}([\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_{6}]^{3-}/[\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_{6}]^{4-}) = +0.36 \text{ V}$$ The more positive value is the stronger oxidant.

Test each oxidant against iodide**
For $\text{Fe}^{3+}$: $E^{\ominus}_{cell} = 0.77 - 0.54 = +0.23 \text{ V}$, positive so reaction occurs. For the complex: $E^{\ominus}_{cell} = 0.36 - 0.54 = -0.18 \text{ V}$, negative so no reaction. Ligands change the $E^{\ominus}$ of iron dramatically.

Final answer: $E^{\ominus}$ $\text{I}_{2}$/$\text{I}^{-}$ = +0.54 V, $\text{Fe}^{3+}$/$\text{Fe}^{2+}$ = +0.77 V, $[\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_{6}]^{3-}$/$[\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_{6}]^{4-}$ = +0.36 V.
$E^{\ominus}_{cell}$ = +0.23 V for $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ oxidising $\text{I}^{-}$ so feasible, $E^{\ominus}_{cell}$ = -0.18 V for $[\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_{6}]^{3-}$ oxidising $\text{I}^{-}$ so not feasible.

hints: Look at the charges on $\text{S}_{2}\text{O}_{8}^{2-}$ and tartrate $\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{4}\text{O}_{6}^{2-}$ and think about bringing them together.
walkthrough:
Visualise the collision**
Both reactants are $2-$ anions. To react they must collide, but like charges repel strongly. Few collisions have enough energy to overcome this repulsion, so activation energy is high and the uncatalysed rate is very slow. $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ cations avoid this problem.
Final answer: Both $\text{S}_{2}\text{O}_{8}^{2-}$ and tartrate ions are negatively charged so repel each other, giving a high $E_{a}$ and very slow reaction.

hints: Balance the given skeleton with water, $\text{H}^{+}$ and electrons to balance O, H and charge for the oxidation of tartrate.
walkthrough:
Balance as an oxidation half-equation**
Tartrate is oxidised to carbon dioxide and methanoate. Oxygen is balanced with $2\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ on the left, hydrogen with $6\text{H}^{+}$ on the right, and charge with $6\text{e}^{-}$ on the right: $$\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{4}\text{O}_{6}^{2-} + 2\text{H}_{2}\text{O} \rightleftharpoons 2\text{CO}_{2} + 2\text{HCO}_{2}^{-} + 6\text{H}^{+} + 6\text{e}^{-}$$ Check atoms and charge balance carefully.

hints: Recall what $\text{LiAlH}_{4}$ does to a carboxylic acid group and whether alcohol groups are affected.
Recall which groups in tartaric acid react with $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCl}$ and what small molecule is lost when an ester forms.
Name the reaction types, one is gain of hydrogen to form alcohol, the other joins molecules with loss of $\text{HCl}$.
walkthrough:
Reduce with $\text{LiAlH}_{4}$**
$\text{LiAlH}_{4}$ is a powerful reducing agent that converts each $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ to a primary alcohol $\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$, while the existing secondary $\text{OH}$ groups are unchanged. Tartaric acid $\text{HO}_{2}\text{CCH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ therefore gives the tetraol: $$\text{HOCH}_{2}\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$$ This is reduction.

Esterify with $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCl}$**
Acyl chlorides esterify alcohol groups rapidly but do not attack carboxylic acids under these conditions without heating. The two $\text{OH}$ groups become ethanoate esters: $$\text{HO}_{2}\text{CCH}(\text{OCOCH}_{3})\text{CH}(\text{OCOCH}_{3})\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$$ $\text{HCl}$ is eliminated, so this is condensation (esterification).

Complete the table**
Ensure structures show all functional groups clearly and both reaction types are named correctly to earn all three marks.

Final answer: With excess $\text{LiAlH}_{4}$: $\text{HOCH}_{2}\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$, reduction.
With excess $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCl}$: $\text{HO}_{2}\text{CCH}(\text{OCOCH}_{3})\text{CH}(\text{OCOCH}_{3})\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$, condensation.

hints: Think of tartaric acid donating a proton to the amine, forming a carboxylate anion and an alkylammonium cation.
walkthrough:
Form the ammonium salt**
The amine $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}(\text{NH}_{2})\text{CH}_{3}$ is a base and tartaric acid is an acid. One $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ transfers $\text{H}^{+}$ to $\text{NH}_{2}$ to give $\text{NH}_{3}^{+}$. The product is an ion pair: carboxylate anion with ammonium cation, $$\text{HO}_{2}\text{CCH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CO}_{2}^{-} \text{ C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}(\text{NH}_{3}^{+})\text{CH}_{3}$$ A dianion with two ammonium cations is also acceptable.
Final answer: $\text{HO}_{2}\text{CCH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CO}_{2}^{-}$ $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}(\text{NH}_{3}^{+})\text{CH}_{3}$
